title: Ashton Jeanty Hops on the Bust‑Train: From NFL Dreams to Trades‑Ville Triumph
body:
The Las Vegas Raiders’ once‑heralded 2025 first‑round selection, running back Ashton Jeannette, has rapidly become a cautionary tale of draft optimism gone awry, as the former college star struggles to find footing in the NFL and appears destined for a role far removed from the franchise’s high‑profile expectations. After two lackluster seasons, the 23‑year‑old has been relegated to the practice squad and is now reportedly exploring a move to the Canadian Football League, prompting analysts to label him one of the league’s most glaring busts.

When the Raiders pulled the trigger on Jeannette with the sixth overall pick, the decision was lauded as a masterstroke. The player arrived in Las Vegas on the back of a stellar junior‑year campaign at a Power Five university, where he amassed over 1,800 rushing yards, 22 touchdowns, and showcased a blend of breakaway speed and bruising power that few NFL scouts believed could be replicated at the professional level. The organization’s front office, eager to revitalize a stagnant ground game, framed the selection as a long‑term investment that would anchor the offense for years to come.

Reality, however, has proven less forgiving. In his rookie season, Jeannette logged a meager 312 rushing yards on 84 carries, averaging just 3.7 yards per attempt, and failed to record a single touchdown. The following year saw marginal improvement—483 yards and three scores—but both figures fell well short of the 1,000‑yard benchmark typically expected of top‑ten picks. Moreover, his pass‑catching ability, once touted as a secondary weapon, has remained underutilized, with a total of 22 receptions for 180 yards across two seasons. Critics point to a combination of factors: a crowded backfield that limited snaps, a coaching staff that struggled to adapt the playbook to his skill set, and lingering injuries that hampered his development.

The Raiders’ management has attempted to address the situation through roster shuffling and coaching changes, yet the underlying issue appears to be a mismatch between Jeannette’s college production and the demands of an NFL pro‑style offense. While his physical attributes—5‑11, 215 pounds, and a 4.44‑second 40‑yard dash—remain impressive, his vision in the open field and ability to break tackles against elite defenders have been called into question. Video analysis from the past season highlights a pattern of hesitancy at the line of scrimmage and a tendency to over‑commit to cutback lanes that are quickly sealed by disciplined defensive fronts.

The broader implications of Jeannette’s decline reverberate beyond Las Vegas. His case fuels ongoing debates about the efficacy of early‑round selections on the running back position, a topic that has gained traction as teams increasingly favor passing attacks and view backs as interchangeable commodities. The Raiders’ miscalculation also underscores the perils of over‑relying on collegiate statistics without adequately considering scheme fit and the transitional challenges of the professional game. As other franchises observe the fallout, there may be a measurable shift toward valuing versatility and pass‑catching proficiency over pure rushing prowess in future drafts.

Looking ahead, Jeannette faces a pivotal crossroads. If he embraces a move to a league where his skill set can be leveraged—potentially the CFL or a developmental arena like the XFL—he could resurrect his career and demonstrate the playmaking ability that once made him a coveted prospect. For the Raiders, the situation serves as a stark reminder to calibrate draft strategies with realistic assessments of player adaptability and to invest in developmental resources that can bridge the gap between college dominance and NFL readiness. The next chapter of Jeannette’s football journey will be closely watched, offering both a potential redemption story and a lesson in the high stakes of draft day decisions.
